extra.source_text: Back to Articles Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Team Article Published October 13, 2026 Upvote 64 +58 Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Teacher specialization Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks. MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Benchmark results We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters. Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61 BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78 ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13 LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72 PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20 τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01 WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69 GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42 AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58 HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65 IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19 IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67 Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34 MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40 SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40 SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78 *All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters. For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads. These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. Inference speed on CPU and GPU LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX. Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300. How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0 ): pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map= "auto" , dtype= "bfloat16" , # attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt= True , skip_special_tokens= True ) prompt = "What is C. elegans?" input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : prompt}], add_generation_prompt= True , return_tensors= "pt" , tokenize= True , )[ "input_ids" ].to(model.device) output = model.generate( input_ids, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.05 , max_new_tokens= 512 , streamer=streamer, ) Use it in your agent harness Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent: hermes config set model.provider custom hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1 hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B hermes config set model.context_length 131072 hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080 , vLLM uses 8000 , SGLang uses 30000 , and LM Studio uses 1234 . See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples. Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-24B-A2B to your task with our fine-tuning tutorials . We can't wait to see what you build. extra.source_text: Engineering How the Claude Code team does code review How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents. AUTHOR Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang CATEGORY Engineering PUBLISHED Oct 15, 2026 READING TIME 14 min We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it? This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent. We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year. Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible. Code review does two jobs: Find and fix issues before they ship Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end. We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily. Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second. So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it. THE LIFE OF A CHANGE A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review. Few get through all of them, and rollback handles the rest. 1. The work is verified before anyone else looks Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide . Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines. Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator." When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as: CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date. REVIEW.md , written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix. 2. AI review on every pull request Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else? On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code , is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally. When we launched the research preview , the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time. Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault. Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round. 3. Security review that can block Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive. If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code . 4. Automated checks that block The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here .) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it. 5. Human approval, scaled by risk A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review. Risk Examples Human approvals Low Docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flag None required once automated review and security checks are green Medium Ordinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system prompts One person High The highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two people Two people The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file. Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human. Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves. An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again. 6. tools.headline: Anthropic built its own source control system, Scion, to handle AI-written code
tools.summary: Anthropic now merges over 30,000 code changes a day, so it built Scion to replace git for its giant codebase.
tools.why_it_matters: If your projects grow fast with AI help, git's old design may hit the same limits, and this post explains why.

extra.source_text: Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion. At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned. Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard. As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones. The typical setup for scaling git checkouts. Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like? Principles for agent-scale source control With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling , 2 so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are: Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it. Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally. A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control. Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed. Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem. The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads. How Scion works It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle. Data structures In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, 1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly. The shape of a changeset in Scion. This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets. A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents. This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search. Scaling Scion A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner. Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own. Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want. In the fleet, the client talk

tools.headline: DeepSeek Search and Fetch: pay per request to let AI tools read live web pages
tools.summary: Search finds pages for a query, and Fetch turns one page into clean Markdown text, both for $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests.
tools.why_it_matters: Your AI helper can look up fresh web info without you building a scraper, and failed or empty searches cost nothing.
tools.for_builders: Send a POST to https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search with your API key as a Bearer token and a JSON body containing a query.

extra.candidate_title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
extra.source_text: On this page Search & Fetch The Search API and the Fetch API give agents and RAG applications access to live web content: Search API finds web pages for a query and returns structured results. It is powered by DeepSeek's in-house search engine. Fetch API retrieves a single web page and returns its content as Markdown. Both are raw JSON APIs. They use the same bearer authentication as the DeepSeek API. The base URL is https://api.deepseek.com : API Endpoint Search POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search Fetch POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch See the Search API Reference and Fetch API Reference for the complete request and response schemas. Authentication ​ Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers: Header Required Value Authorization Yes Bearer <DeepSeek API Key> Content-Type Yes application/json Search API ​ Request ​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "query": "DeepSeek V4 release", "count": 5, "need_content": true }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "query" : "DeepSeek V4 release" , "count" : 5 , "need_content" : True , } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) for result in response . json ( ) [ "results" ] : print ( result [ "title" ] , result [ "url" ] ) print ( result [ "summary" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Default Description query string Yes - The search query must contain 1 to 128 Unicode characters, cannot be all whitespace, and supports the query operators listed below. count integer No 10 The number of results to return, between 1 and 50. ori_question string No - The user's original question that triggered the search, between 1 and 128 characters, to improve query understanding, with null treated as not provided. localization string No "" An optional IP address used to localize search results. need_content boolean No false Whether to return page content in content , which is always an empty string when false . Unknown fields in the request body are ignored. Query Operators ​ The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query. Operator Example Description site: DeepSeek site:github.com Restrict results to the given site, and to target multiple sites, separate the site: clauses with spaces and join them with OR , for example DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co . -site: DeepSeek -site:example.com Exclude the given site, and separate multiple sites with spaces. - DeepSeek -advertisement Exclude pages containing the term, and separate multiple terms with spaces. -"..." DeepSeek -"release notes" Exclude pages containing the exact phrase, which can contain spaces, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. "..." DeepSeek "exact phrase" Match an exact phrase, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. lang: DeepSeek lang:zh,en Restrict results to the given language codes, separating multiple codes with commas, for example lang:zh,en . after: DeepSeek after:2025 or DeepSeek after:2025-01-01 Restrict results to pages published after a date. before: DeepSeek before:2026 or DeepSeek before:2026-06-01 Restrict results to pages published before a date. For example: { "query": "DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co lang:en after:2025", "count": 10 } Response ​ A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a results array. A normal search with no matches returns an empty array. { "results": [ { "rerank_score": 2.4, "title": "DeepSeek V4 model released", "url": "https://example.com/deepseek-v4", "snippet": "DeepSeek V4 is now available, with tool calling and long-context support.", "summary": "DeepSeek has released the V4 model. The release adds improved tool calling and long-context support for agent workflows.", "content": "DeepSeek V4 is now generally available...", "site_name": "Example News", "site_icon": "https://example.com/favicon.ico", "date": "2026-06-01T00:00:00+00:00", "authority": 3 } ] } Each item in results contains: Field Type Description rerank_score number A relevance score from 0 to 3 that combines signals such as relevance, authority, and freshness, with scores of 1.5 or above considered high-quality results. title string The title of the result. url string The URL of the result. snippet string A short summary related to the query, typically 100 to 200 characters, intended for display in a UI. summary string A long summary related to the query, typically 600 to 800 characters, intended to be read by a model. content string The page content, which is empty when need_content is false or when the content is unavailable. site_name string or null The name of the site, or null when unavailable. site_icon string or null The URL of the site icon, or null when unavailable. date string or null The publication time in UTC, formatted as RFC 3339, or null when unknown. authority integer The authority tier of the page, 0 to 4 ( -1 means unknown), with values of 3 or above indicating highly authoritative sources. Fetch API ​ Request ​ curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "url": "https://example.com/article" }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "url" : "https://example.com/article" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) page = response . json ( ) print ( page [ "title" ] ) print ( page [ "content" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Description url string Yes The page URL to fetch, which must be at most 8192 characters, an HTTP or HTTPS URL with a host, and must not contain a username or password. Response ​ { "title": "Example article", "content": "# Example article\n\nArticle content." } Field Type Description title string The title of the page, empty when the title is unavailable. content string The fetched page content as Markdown text. Fetching is subject to the target site's availability and access policies. Errors ​ Errors follow the OpenAI-compatible error format. The param field is always null . { "error": { "message": "'count' must be between 1 and 50", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": null, "code": "invalid_request_error" } } HTTP Status Description 400 The request headers or body are invalid, including malformed JSON or an invalid field value. 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 402 The account has insufficient balance. 403 The Fetch request was rejected by the security policy. 404 Fetch could not retrieve usable page content, for example due to an unavailable URL, a URL blocked by site policy, an error from the target site, an unsupported content type, or a page with no extractable Markdown content. 408 Reading the request body timed out. 413 The request body is too large. 429 The Search or Fetch QPS limit was exceeded. 500 An internal server error occurred. 504 A downstream request timed out. Search and Fetch are read-only. For HTTP 408, 429, or 5xx errors, wait and retry. For HTTP 402, top up your account before retrying. Do not retry other 4xx errors without changing the request. Billing ​ Search and Fetch are billed per successful request, not by tokens or by the number of returned results: API Unit Price Search Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 Fetch Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 A request is billable only when it returns HTTP 200 and produces a result (Search must return a non-empty results array, and Fetch must return page content). Failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request price. Note: when you use the DeepSeek API through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex, server-side tool calls already hit the Search and Fetch APIs. These calls are currently free of charge; per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026. Rate Limits ​ For each account, Search and Fetch are limited independently, and traffic to one does not consume the other's quota: API QPS Limit Search 5 Fetch 5 The QPS (requests per second) limits are calculated at the account level, regardless of which API key is used, and are separate from the model concurrency limits. Requests above the account-level QPS limit receive HTTP 429. In addition to the account-level limit, Fetch is also subject to a per-domain QPS limit, and requests above that limit also receive HTTP 429.

tools.headline: Codex CLI runs a background daemon by default, and users want it opt-in
tools.summary: Since version 0.157.0, opening Codex can start a background process that keeps running after you close the window and checks for updates hourly.
tools.why_it_matters: If you launch Codex with a proxy setting, the background process may keep using the first session's proxy, even in later sessions.
tools.for_builders: Run codex features disable daemon_auto_start, then codex app-server daemon stop to stop the background process.

Understand how it works, down to the binary level.** [![npm version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/rea-agents?style=flat-square&color=cb3837)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/rea-agents) [![MCP tool catalog](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-tool_catalog-5c4ee5?style=flat-square)](docs/mcp-contracts.md#generated-catalog) [![Node.js requirements](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-requirements-339933?style=flat-square&logo=nodedotjs&logoColor=white)](#what-you-can-analyze) [![skills.sh](https://skills.sh/b/morluto/rea?style=flat-square)](https://skills.sh/morluto/rea/reverse-engineer-anything) [![MIT license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-f4c430?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1556595354999332884?logo=discord&logoColor=white&label=Discord&color=5865F2)](https://discord.gg/GkcryMnJDM) **[Website](https://rea.tools/) · [Guides](https://rea.tools/guides/) · [Showcases](https://rea.tools/showcase/)** [Quick start](#quick-start) · [How REA works](#how-rea-works) · [What you can analyze](#what-you-can-analyze) · [Showcases](#showcases) · [FAQ](#faq) · [Documentation](#documentation) npx rea-agents setup
> [!IMPORTANT] > Get REA from [morluto/rea](https://github.com/morluto/rea), > [rea.tools](https://rea.tools/), or the [rea-agents npm package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/rea-agents). > Follow the installation and release links from these official sources. A similar > repository name or copied README does not establish that a download is official.




Join the Reverse Engineering Community
Discord · Q&A · Show and Tell

--- See a feature in an app that you want in your own product? Ask your agent to investigate it with REA. It can inspect the app without its source code, explain how the feature works, show the evidence, and build a version for your project. REA connects your agent to tools for inspecting native binaries, JavaScript and Electron apps, .NET assemblies, and websites. You can also use the same tools from your terminal. Analysis runs locally, and results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions. Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval. Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine. > **[Visit the REA website](https://rea.tools/)** for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies. ## Quick start On Linux, Ghidra, JADX, firmware tool launches and static JavaScript/Electron analysis require a procps-compatible `ps` on REA's `PATH` for process ownership checks. Recovery steps are in `docs/installation.md` under "Linux owned-process prerequisite". ### Set up your agent With Node.js and npm installed, run: ```bash npx rea-agents setup ``` Choose your agents, review the proposed changes, and approve them. Setup adds REA's MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration. Restart your agent afterward. Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and [other agents](docs/installation.md#supported-agents). See [installation and setup](docs/installation.md) for provider configuration and manual MCP registration. ### Ask your agent ```text Understand how search works in the Notes app, show me the evidence, and build a similar feature for my project. ``` Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand. ### Use the terminal Inspect an extracted JavaScript/Electron app directory or ASAR: ```bash npx -y rea-agents@latest analyze-javascript-application /absolute/path/to/app --json ``` The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence. Replace the path with your target, such as `"D:/apps/example"` on Windows. To install the `rea` command for regular use: ```bash npm install --global rea-agents rea --help ``` For native analysis, configure a provider first. See the [CLI and Evidence guide](docs/cli.md) for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting. ### Update REA REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes. Keep your installation up to date. For a CLI installed with `npm install --global` or `bun add --global`: ```bash rea update ``` `rea --update` is an alias for this verified workflow and accepts the same global output flags. Use `rea update` when combining it with other command controls. Updater commands retain at most 4 MiB of stdout and stderr combined. Oversized metadata replies are rejected after the command exits; verbose installs continue with bounded diagnostics. Human progress output respects terminal backpressure and waits for submitted writes to finish. Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later. With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running `rea update`. To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update. If you use `npx`, update your agent setup with: ```bash npx rea-agents@latest setup ``` Review the setup changes and restart your agent. For one-off CLI commands, use `npx rea-agents@latest` followed by the command. With Bun, use `bunx rea-agents@latest` in place of `npx rea-agents@latest`. ## How REA works Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with their evidence. The agent uses them to ask follow-up questions, explain the behavior, or write and test an implementation. CLI commands use the same workflows. ![REA investigation flow: your agent asks about a local target, REA inspects and traces it using analysis tools, and the agent uses the returned code, references and unknowns to explain, implement and test.](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg) [Open the full-size figure](website/public/assets/figures/rea-investigation-flow.svg). ## What you can analyze REA requires Node.js 22.x (>=22.19), 24.x (>=24.11), or 26+, plus npm. --- ## 交流群

QQ 群：386179533（AI 技术交流学习群）
扫码加入群聊，一起交流插件使用心得、反馈问题与分享玩法。
--- ## 亮点 - **开箱即用，无配置环节**——不需要账号、不需要 Key、不需要在后台申请配额。 - **上游来源公开透明**——免费车道来源为 [OpenCode 的 Zen 网关](https://opencode.ai)，Kilo 渠道来源为 [Kilo AI 的公共网关](https://kilo.ai)，均直连、不经任何第三方中转。请求由谁处理、数据发往何处，见「上游是哪些源」与「免责声明」。 - **清单跟随上游**——模型集合、上下文长度与能力在每次刷新时向上游重新拉取，插件内不保存静态快照。 - **选择器只广播可用的模型**——上游清单已声明但网关明确拒绝路由的模型（返回 `Model is unavailable`、或 404 找不到该 id）从下拉框移除，仅在设置页保留记录并注明拒因；网关自身故障（5xx）、配额限制（429）、超时与断网不属于对模型的判定，一律保持可达；被地区策略拦截的模型归入 region-limited 分组。整轮探测全部被拒时同样保留，选择器不会为空。 - **公告中心 + 实时推送**——仓库维护者在仓库中编辑 JSON 并推送后，所有已安装实例最迟在一个轮询周期内收到；正文为白名单约束下的 HTML，支持图文排版；`urgent` 级别触发全屏弹窗；可选系统级通知。 - **应用内升级**——设置页一键升级：下载 → SHA-256 校验 → 备份 → 原子替换 → 校验回读 → 热重载，任一步失败自动回滚至上一版本。 - **热重载**——升级与代码变更即时生效，无需重启应用；也可在设置页手动触发，或启用文件监视自动重载。 - **按响应体形状判定流式响应**——网关在高负载下会以 `application/json` 的 content-type 返回完整的 SSE 帧序列。插件按响应体形状判定，并将已嗅探的字节重新注入流，既不会导致整轮失败，也不会因 header 与实际内容不符而将可用模型判为不可用。 - **思考强度实际生效**——两类模型两种控制：声明了思考档位的模型（如 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash、GLM 5.3 Flash）给出它自己的档位菜单（Off / Low / High / Max 等），选中值按原值下发到上游 `reasoning_effort`，上游会校验该字段、集合外的取值直接 400；没有档位菜单的模型（MiMo V2.6 等）走预算阶梯——Light / Balanced / Deep 对应输出 token 预算 2 048 / 8 192 / 模型上限，思考不可关闭的模型三档整体翻倍为 4 096 / 16 384 / 模型上限，因为思考与正文共享同一输出额度。两者都逐次调用留痕，设置页每张模型卡均标注档位或该档实际下发的上限（详见「思考强度：档位菜单与预算阶梯」）。 - **不依赖浏览器界面**——插件仅将 llm 作为硬依赖，在没有 web server 的 composition（如 dsh-tui）中同样完成启动并输出模型；看板模块挂载在独立的 fiber 上，待 webServer 就绪后再注册路由，因此既不会阻塞模型车道，也不会因插件先于 web 服务加载而永久丢失设置页。 - **用量看板，数据全部留在本机**——Token 热力图、总量曲线（支持总计与单模型视图）、输出速度与首字延迟逐次采样。不上传任何数据。 - **OpenAI 兼容转发端口**——本机其它工具通过 base URL 与 Key 即可调用这些模型。 - **EAC 渠道（桌面端专属）**——在 DeepSeek Harness 桌面端与 DSHEAC AIO 桌面端中自动解锁一条协付通道，模型以 EAC 前缀显示（如 EAC DeepSeek V4.1 Flash）；凭据加密密封，由宿主指纹闸门把守；该渠道在服务器侧校验 GitHub 授权（登录并 star 本仓库）后才放行对话；在命令行及其它宿主中该通道完全不存在。详见「EAC 渠道」。 - **Kilo 渠道（免密免费池）**——内置 Kilo AI 公共网关的免费模型池（`isFree` 清单实时拉取，含 `kilo-auto/free` 自动路由），无需任何账号或 Key；模型卡带 Kilo 徽章。思考强度与 EAC 渠道同款：模型自身的档位菜单（Off / Low / Medium / High，默认 High），经网关统一的 `reasoning` 参数真实下发——Off 已逐家族实测将思考归零（nemotron、ling、dots、poolside、apodex、cohere）；stepfun 与 liquid 端点强制思考（对关闭请求返回 400）、两个自动路由不透传关闭，这些模型的菜单不含 Off 档。该池由上游免费提供，上游会在其模型卡中声明 prompt 可能被记录用于改进服务——请勿发送敏感内容，详见「免责声明」。 - **聚合渠道，自带 Key**——设置页新增一页，把第三方端点接进同一条模型清单：注册表内置 75 家提供商（NVIDIA NIM、OpenRouter、Groq、Cerebras、SambaNova、Gemini、DeepSeek、Mistral、Together、Fireworks、SiliconFlow、Nebius、Chutes、Hugging Face、Cloudflare、Z.ai、Kimi、MiniMax、QwenCloud/Alibaba、Bedrock、Vertex、Vercel AI Gateway、Azure OpenAI，以及无需账号的 Ollama、LM Studio、llama.cpp），写入 Key（本机免账号的提供商不需要）后其模型即以 `provider/model` 出现在选择器里，也可经本地网关调用。Key 只写入本机 0600 的 settings.json，API 只回显 `hasKey` 与 `…abcd` 指纹；每家可单独启停、测试（列表探测，不花一次生成）、发现模型、覆盖 Base URL 与模型清单。OAuth 与 ADC 认证的提供商照常列出，但标注为不可驱动。 - **省 Token**——三件事：工具输出压缩（RTK）在请求发出前就地重写 `tool_result`（git diff / status / log、grep、find、ls、tree、构建日志、编号转储、搜索清单、重复日志行），实测 40 KB 的 `git diff` 移除 90% 的字节且模型仍能就它作答；提示词瘦身有 caveman 与 ponytail 两族、默认全关；另有五个不占用上游请求的本地应答。设置页用与用量图表同一批统计行显示压缩前后字节、节省比例、压缩块数与统计调用数。 - **路由（降级链）**——把任意车道的模型串成一条命名链，以 `combo:` 作为虚拟模型出现在选择器与网关上；`fallback` 固定从链首开始，`round-robin` 轮换起点并连续 N 轮粘滞。链接在输出任何正文之前失败会被整段丢弃，切换对调用方不可见；思考增量不算正文，因此「想了很久才撞上配额墙」正是降级最有价值的场景。 - **本地网关原生说 Anthropic**——新增 `POST /v1/messages`（流式与非流式，含 thinking / tool_use 块、真实 stop_reason 与流内 error 事件）与 `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens`（本地估算）；`/v1/models` 广播全部车道，含聚合行与链路。网关页新增「接入客户端」分区，按实际绑定的端口与真实要求的密钥生成 Claude Code、Codex、OpenAI SDK、Anthropic SDK、curl 与局域网的可复制配方。 - **接口具备鉴权围栏**——插件 HTTP 路由优先级高于内核 `/api`，因此内置与内核一致的信任检查（优先复用 composition 的 connection 服务，缺失时退回结构化围栏）。 - **十三个白嫖渠道，一体接入**——CodeArts（华为云）、CodeBuddy / WorkBuddy（腾讯）、LobsterAI（有道）、Qoder / Qoder 中国版（阿里系）、TRAE（字节）、Cline、Loomy（讯飞）、Raccoon（商汤）、MiniMax Code、ZCode（智谱）、Gemini（Google Code Assist）十一个账号渠道开箱即用，外加 Kilo 免费车道与原匿名免费通道；OpenCode 账号渠道在本插件中默认停用。各渠道的登录流程、账号池、每日积分领取、模型黑名单与其本地 OpenAI 网关（Chat Completions + Responses，默认 `127.0.0.1:8326`）原样挂载与运行；凭据只写入宿主凭据库，浏览器永远拿不到明文。 - **十一页毛玻璃界面**——设置页顶部导航扩为十一个页面：原有六页（**免费模型**（鱼缸水位 = 可用模型占比）、**EAC 模型**（鱼缸水位 = 协付池压力）、**白嫖模型接入**（十三张渠道卡：登录、账号、模型开关、一键领取积分）、**数据看板**（今日/全部 Token 消耗、平均生成速度、缓存命中率、成功率，账号透视与模型性能表、最近请求总览）、**运行日志**（逐请求明细：结果、耗时、首字、速度、Token 细分，失败原因悬停可见）与**网关设置**（网关开关/端点/密钥；局域网转发中继：监听地址、端口与独立中继密钥）），新增**聚合渠道**（提供商注册表、Key、测试、发现模型、Base URL 与模型清单覆盖）、**省 Token**（压缩开关、两族提示词档位、五个本地应答与节省统计）、**路由**（降级链编辑器）、**插件升级**（版本检查、一键升级与热重载）与**推荐项目**（EAC-Desktop / EAC-Pack / EAC-design-world 三张卡片：简介、直达链接与 Star 按钮，Star / Fork / 最近提交数实时取自 GitHub，取不到就整块不显示）五页；网关设置页另增「接入客户端」分区。页面切换与卡片入场为 150–250 ms 短动效，`prefers-reduced-motion` 下整体关闭。每页都有直达 GitHub 仓库的 Star 按钮。 - **局域网转发中继**——渠道网关本身只监听本机（上游的安全选择）；本插件提供自己的转发门：调用方用插件签发与轮换的中继密钥，转发跳由宿主换用网关凭据（凭据不出宿主进程），仅放行 `/v1/*` 模型接口并带环路保护。 ## 你会看到什么 **输入框的模型选择器** | 分组 | 内容 | | --- | --- | | Our Free Model | 当前网络出口可直接使用的模型 | | Our Free Model · region-limited | 上游对该地区不放行的模型，保留可见但单独隔离 | 被判定为「已声明但不路由」的模型不出现在任何分组中——它们仅在设置页的「不在选择器中」分组保留记录， 附带拒因与探测时间；后续探测重新通过后自动回到选择器。 **设置页** 设置 → Our Free Model，包含七个分区： - **模型清单**——各模型的可用性、是否支持视觉、上下文窗口、最长输出、各思考档位实际下发的输出上限、实测首字延迟，以及单次调用基准测试按钮。 - **EAC 渠道授权**——一键发起 GitHub 登录（自动打开浏览器，无需复制粘贴）、显示登录名与 star 校验状态、重新检查、退出登录；未授权时模型卡带锁标记。免费车道的模型不受影响。 - **公告中心**——仓库维护者推送的公告流：未读计数、紧急徽章、单条/全部标记已读、检查新公告按钮、系统通知开关。公告正文按白名单渲染 HTML。 - **用量看板**——总览计数、17 周 Token 热力图、总量曲线（Token / 请求数切换，总计与单模型切换）、速度迷你图、按模型汇总表。 - **本地转发**——开关、监听地址与端口、复制 base URL、显示 / 复制 / 轮换 API Key，并提供可直接执行的 curl 示例。 - **插件设置**——总开关、是否展示地区受限模型、探测间隔、默认输出上限，以及当前探测到的出口 IP 与国家。 - **插件升级**——当前/最新版本、检查更新、一键升级（含进度与失败原因）、最近一次升级历史、热重载按钮与文件监视开关。 - **首次启动公告**——分 5 页（前言 / 模型清单 / 使用步骤 / 功能介绍 / 公告与升级），确认一次后不再弹出，除非文案版本号被提升。 ## 独立本地服务（开发中） 仓库现在提供两个入口：下文安装的是 **DSH 插件**；`packages/standalone` 是 **无需安装 DSH 的独立本地服务**。从完整源码仓库运行： ```powershell npm run start:standalone ``` 独立服务默认使用 `~/.our-free-model` 和端口 `18900`，拥有自己的 API Key， 不读取插件数据。支持匿名/Kilo、EAC 和原有十三个账号渠道，提供 Chat Completions、Responses API，以及独立网页管理（模型、统计、渠道、EAC、设置、API Key）。 启动后打开终端打印的一次性管理链接即可使用；账号在独立页面登录，也可手动导入插件账号备份。 启动、参数与验证见 [独立服务说明](packages/standalone/README.md)。 独立服务的安装制品与 Release 尚未发布。 ## 安装 > **⚠️ 不要通过 npm 安装本插件。** > > npm 上的 `dsh-our-free-model` 包**不是本仓库发布的**。它由第三方打包，内容与本仓库 > 不一致：`index.js`、`client.js` 被改动，并额外包含本仓库从未有过的 > `src/channel-visibility.js`。装到它得不到本项目审核过的构建，也拿不到本仓库的签名 > 清单校验与应用内升级。 > > 请只按本文档下方的方式安装：使用本仓库的 Release 发布包，或本地源码目录。 > 其它渠道出现的同名包一律以本仓库为准。 **命令行（纯 dsh web）** ``` dsh plugin --profile web add /绝对路径/dsh-our-free-model ``` 安装完成后重启应用一次。`--profile` 填写实际使用的 profile 名称。 **DSHEAC AIO / 桌面端：请先阅读本节** 部分 DSHEAC AIO / 旧版桌面整合包在启动 web 服务之前会执行 profile 闸门， 限制 profile 中的符号链接或目录 junction。若当前宿主包含该检查，可能报错： ``` PROFILE_UPGRADE_REQUIRED: offline dependency migration is not yet available ``` 遇到该闸门时，不要使用 `link:` 依赖或 junction；使用应用内插件管理器， 或下方的本地 tarball 安装。不同宿主的限制以自身日志和安装机制为准。 以真实目录手工安装时，使用可信源码打出的本地 tarball： 1. 创建 `/profiles//vendor/`，在审核过的本仓库目录运行 `npm pack --ignore-scripts --pack-destination "/profiles//vendor"`，或将本仓库正式发布的同版本 tarball 放入该目录。本地打包不执行 npm 发布。 2. 在 profile 的 `package.json` 的 dependencies 中加入 `"dsh-our-free-model": "file:./vendor/dsh-our-free-model-2.5.3.tgz"`。文件名版本跟随仓库 `package.json`，不要改成同名 npm 注册表版本；再通过宿主的安装流程解析依赖。 3. 在 dsh.profile.bundles 末尾追加 `"dsh-our-free-model"`。 包管理器拥有这份安装的字节时，同时将 bundle config 或插件 `settings.json` 的 `distribution` 设为 `managed`，由包管理器统一更新；应用内升级、公告 feed 与热重载会停用，模型功能保留。以后更新时替换可信 tarball 并同步依赖路径，避免包管理器按旧锁文件恢复旧版本。 若手工复制发布文件，必须复制完整包，包括 `adapter/`、`src/`、`locale/` 和 `vendor/channel-pack/` 下的 `pack.js`、WASM、LICENSE、NOTICE；只复制入口脚本会导致渠道加载失败。 不要再向 cordis.patch.yml 添加条目。被 dsh.profile.bundles 引用的包，其自带的 patch 层会自动生效；两处同时注册将报错 duplicate loader entry id: our-free-model。 **整合包（托管安装）** 插件由整合包（EAC 整合包、Mojobox 等）安装时，更新时机与文件字节由安装方控制： 安装时将 bundle config 设为 distribution: 'managed'（或向 settings.json 写入 同一字段），插件的应用内升级、公告 feed 与热重载即全部停用——两个写入方同时操作 同一安装目录只会导致目录损坏；模型 lane 不受影响。相关验收见 scripts/offline-test.mjs；目录就绪记录（manifest 0.15 / 出处 / 许可 / 完整性） 位于 catalog/ 下。 **启动桌面端前的自检** 可直接调用桌面端自身的闸门代码进行自检： ``` node -e " const g = require('/sidecar/dist/lib/profile-upgrade.js'); const app = '', profile = '/profiles/'; console.log(g.planProfileUpgrade(app, profile)); g.assertProfileStartup(app, profile); console.log('startup gate: PASS'); " ``` 预期输出为 status: 'compatible'、mismatches 为空数组，随后输出 PASS。 若仅需确认 bundle 组合是否正确而不启动界面： ``` DSH_HOME= dsh --profile --dump-config | grep our-free-model ``` 应当只出现一个 id: our-free-model。 **安装失败：ERR_PNPM_VIRTUAL_STORE_DIR_MAX_LENGTH_DIFF** 该问题源于目标 profile 的 pnpm 状态，与插件仓库无关（报错发生在下载插件之前）：profile 中已有的 node_modules 由旧版 pnpm 生成，dsh 更新后内置的 pnpm 版本发生变化，pnpm 拒绝在旧参数上继续安装。 关闭 dsh，删除该 profile 的 node_modules 与 pnpm-lock.yaml 使其重建，然后重新安装： ``` rd /s /q "%DSH_HOME%\profiles\web\node_modules" del "%DSH_HOME%\profiles\web\pnpm-lock.yaml" ``` 同时出现的 Ignoring broken lockfile 警告会随重建一同消失。 **安装失败：`git ls-remote "git+ssh://git@github.com/..."`（插件市场自动安装）** 插件市场（dsh-plugin-hub）对 git 源的自动安装会把 GitHub 地址交给 pnpm 解析，pnpm 再调用本机 git 执行 `git ls-remote`。若本机 git 配置了 `insteadOf` 重写（常见于把 https 改写为 ssh 的 `url."git+ssh://git@github.com/".insteadOf` 规则），或 SSH 密钥未配置，这一步会在下载任何插件 文件之前失败。处理方式二选一： - 修正本机 git 配置（`git config --global --get-regexp insteadof` 查看重写规则），保证终端里 `git ls-remote https://github.com/Ebony-Vinyl/dsh-our-free-model.git` 能成功； - 改用本地安装：从 Releases 下载发布包解压后 `dsh plugin add <解压目录>`，绕开 git 解析。 **安装失败：`profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by the Electron application`** 这是宿主自身的保护，不是插件问题：桌面端（Electron）的 profile 只允许桌面应用自己管理， 命令行 `dsh plugin add` 无法写入。请在桌面端的插件管理器（设置 → 插件）里完成安装或升级； 命令行安装仅适用于纯 web profile（`dsh web`）。 ## 桌面安装包（macOS，社区构建） DSH 插件本体无需构建、解压即用；**桌面安装包**（Our Free Model 桌面壳）官方目前只发布 Windows 版。macOS 版为社区构建：源码改动见 [PR #421](https://github.com/Ebony-Vinyl/dsh-our-free-model/pull/421)，可逐行审计；预打好的 Apple Silicon（arm64）包以社区 Release 的版本和校验值为准，也可以自己从源码构建（macOS 上执行 `npm --prefix packages/desktop run build`，完整流水线见 `.github/workflows/build-macos.yml`）。 下载后建议先核对校验和（SHA256 见 PR / Release）： ```bash shasum -a 256 ~/Downloads/Our.Free.Model__aarch64.dmg ``` **安装后提示「已损坏」或打不开？** 社区构建没有 Apple Developer 账号签名与公证，Gatekeeper 会拦截首次启动——这不是文件真的损坏，以下几种方式任选其一： 1. **右键打开**：在访达中按住 Control 点按应用图标，选择「打开」，在弹窗中再次点按「打开」。 2. **清除隔离属性**（终端）： ```bash xattr -cr /Applications/Our\ Free\ Model.app ```

extra.description: An agent skill for creating detailed, interactive isometric illustrations of real-world machines and complex systems. Generates polished SVGs with optional WebGL shaders and 3D effects.
extra.source_text:
An agent skill for creating detailed, interactive isometric illustrations of real-world machines and complex systems. Generates polished SVGs with optional WebGL shaders and 3D effects.

Anatomy

A Claude skill that explains an idea by building it as a real, working object.
Also runs in Antigravity, OpenCode, Codex and MiniMax Code.
Crafted, interactive isometric figures with many small precise parts, in SVG, WebGL and 3D.

   

Quick start · Gallery · What it makes · Install · Usage · Examples · How it works · Limits

examples/raptor-engine, light theme, firing. The engine and stand are SVG; the plume is a WebGL shader in the same isometric camera.

--- Ask Claude for a figure that explains a technical idea, and Anatomy has it invent a physical thing whose working *is* the concept. A cache key that skips work when nothing changed becomes a pin-tumbler lock that only turns when every pin matches. One GPU context serving many canvases becomes a gantry plotter whose single print head visits 16 wells. Then Claude builds that thing out of dozens of small, solid, shaded parts, puts it in a framed card with a title, a hint and a live readout, makes it move calmly under the pointer and the keyboard, and checks its own work by zooming in on every joint. Every number the figure shows comes from the same small model that moves its parts. ## Quick start ```sh npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g ``` The CLI asks which agents to set up (Claude Code, Antigravity, OpenCode, Codex, MiniMax Code). To skip the question, add `-a claude-code`, `-a antigravity`, `-a opencode`, `-a codex`, or `-a minimax-code`. Then, in Claude Code: ```text /anatomy explain how a token bucket rate limiter works, interactive ``` For Antigravity, OpenCode, Codex, or MiniMax Code, target that agent: `-a antigravity`, `-a opencode`, `-a codex`, or `-a minimax-code`. Antigravity, OpenCode and MiniMax Code take the same `/anatomy` command; in Codex, type `$anatomy`. That's it. No API keys and nothing to `npm install`: the kit uses only Node's built-in modules. ## Gallery
raptor-engine: hover to take it apart into 11 assemblies. An audit proves that no pipe passes through anything, at rest, apart and in every frame between. ripple-tank: SVG apparatus over two WebGL layers (lamp light and caustics on the paper, reflections in the water) driven by a dispersion and optics model.
turning-dial: the 3D mode (beta). About 90 parts are re-projected and re-shaded every frame as you drag the dial. dial-indicator: the smallest example, about 300 lines. Hover to slide the carriage; the needle reads each block.
Every screenshot is the light theme of a page in [`examples/`](examples), captured with the skill's own [`scripts/capture.mjs`](scripts/capture.mjs) and [`scripts/drive.mjs`](scripts/drive.mjs). The built pages are committed: open any `.html` in `examples/` to try it. ## What it makes Three kinds of figure. All three share one kit, one camera and one set of craft rules. | Kind | What it is | Example | |---|---|---| | **SVG** | The core. Solid isometric parts with four-tone shading, painted back to front, in a card with a live readout and eased motion. It ships as a standalone HTML page, a lone `.svg` file with its styles embedded, or React/Next.js components. | `dial-indicator`, `desk-computer`, `arcade-cabinet`, `test-rig` | | **SVG + WebGL** | For what lines can't draw: fire, exhaust, water, caustics, lamp light, glow, steam. The shader runs in a canvas between a back and a front SVG, in the figure's own isometric camera, so it sits inside the drawing. The SVG still reads without WebGL. | `raptor-engine`, `ripple-tank` | | **3D** beta | Parts that turn in true 3D: a dial or turntable that spins, fingers that flex, a piece that breaks off and falls. The moving parts are re-projected and re-shaded by the kit's own rules every frame; the rest of the figure stays static art. | `turning-dial` | Each figure is light or dark. Light is the theme the skill designs for first, shaders included. ## Install Anatomy is a standard [Agent Skill](https://agentskills.io): a folder with a `SKILL.md` at its root. This repository is that folder. Pick one way in: | | Command | Installs to | |---|---|---| | **skills CLI**, for you (Claude Code) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a claude-code` | `~/.claude/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for you (Antigravity) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a antigravity` | `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for you (OpenCode) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a opencode` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for you (Codex) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a codex` | `~/.agents/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for you (MiniMax Code) | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a minimax-code` | `~/.minimax/skills/anatomy` | | **skills CLI**, for one project | `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy` | `.claude/skills/anatomy` for Claude Code, `.agents/skills/anatomy` for Antigravity, OpenCode and Codex, `.minimax/skills/anatomy` for MiniMax Code | | **git**, for you (Claude Code) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.claude/skills/anatomy` | `~/.claude/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for you (Antigravity) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` | `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for you (OpenCode) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` | `~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for you (Codex) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.agents/skills/anatomy` | `~/.agents/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for you (MiniMax Code) | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git ~/.minimax/skills/anatomy` | `~/.minimax/skills/anatomy` | | **git**, for one project | `git clone https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy.git .claude/skills/anatomy` | `.claude/skills/anatomy` (Claude Code and OpenCode) or `.agents/skills/anatomy` (Antigravity, OpenCode, Codex and MiniMax Code) | | **Download**, no git | see below | any of the folders above |
With the skills CLI
The [`skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) CLI finds the `SKILL.md` at the root of this repository and installs it as `anatomy`. By default it installs into the current project and asks which agents to set up. `-g` installs it for your user, and `-a claude-code` sets up Claude Code only. Use `-a antigravity`, `-a opencode`, `-a codex` or `-a minimax-code` for Antigravity, OpenCode, Codex or MiniMax Code only. The CLI copies the whole repository, examples included (about 10 MB). It needs a recent Node.js: version 1.7.1 of the CLI asks for 22.20 or later.
With git
Clone the repository into one of the skill folders, so that `SKILL.md` ends up at `/anatomy/SKILL.md`. For Claude Code use `~/.claude/skills/anatomy` or `.claude/skills/anatomy`. For Antigravity use `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/anatomy` or `.agents/skills/anatomy`. For OpenCode use `~/.config/opencode/skills/anatomy` or `.opencode/skills/anatomy`; OpenCode also reads the Claude Code and `.agents` folders. For Codex use `~/.agents/skills/anatomy` or `.agents/skills/anatomy`. For MiniMax Code use `~/.minimax/skills/anatomy` (or `$MINIMAX_DATA_DIR/skills/anatomy` if you moved its data folder) or `.minimax/skills/anatomy`; MiniMax Code also reads the Claude Code, Codex and `.agents` folders. For a project install, commit the folder so your team gets it too. To update later, `git pull` inside that folder.
Download, without git
[Download the ZIP](https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy/archive/refs/heads/main.zip), unpack it, rename the folder from `anatomy-main` to `anatomy`, and move it into `~/.claude/skills/` (Claude Code), `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/` (Antigravity), `~/.config/opencode/skills/` (OpenCode), `~/.agents/skills/` (Codex) or `~/.minimax/skills/` (MiniMax Code). Or in one line on macOS or Linux: ```sh mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/anatomy && curl -L https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy/archive/refs/heads/main.tar.gz | tar -xz --strip-components=1 -C ~/.claude/skills/anatomy ```

The job search that runs on your machine. AI job application framework built on Claude Code: evaluate postings, tailor CVs, write cover letters, prep interviews. Fork it and own it.

# AI Job Search *The job search that runs on your machine.*

[![CI](https://github.com/MadsLorentzen/ai-job-search/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/MadsLorentzen/ai-job-search/actions/workflows/ci.yml) An AI-powered job application framework built on [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code). Fork it, fill in your profile, and let Claude evaluate job postings, tailor your CV, write cover letters, and prepare you for interviews. > Note: This is an independent open-source project and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by, or maintained by Anthropic. Anthropic and Claude Code are referenced only to describe the toolchain this workflow uses. > > This project has **no affiliated cryptocurrency, token, or paid sponsorship program**. Anything claiming otherwise is unauthorized and should be treated as a scam. The only ways to support the project are the Ko-fi link below and contributing on GitHub. ## Does it actually work? I'm a geophysicist by training. When my position was cut in late 2025, I built this framework to run my own job search - the same `/scrape`, `/apply`, and `/interview` workflow in this repo, used weekly, on my own career. I was upfront about it with every employer I spoke to, and instead of counting against me, it usually sparked a genuine technical conversation. Sixty-nine tailored applications, twenty first interviews, and one signed contract later, I started as an AI engineer in June 2026. People kept asking whether this actually works. It got me hired. Now it's yours. *The longer version, including the full application funnel, is on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mads-lorentzen/).*

Did this save you a Sunday of cover-letter writing? Consider a coffee.
Did it land you the job? Maybe two. ☕

## What this is A structured workflow that turns Claude Code into a full-stack job application assistant. The core workflow (self-profiling, fit evaluation, and the drafter-reviewer application pipeline) is **language- and country-agnostic**. The job portal search skills are built for the Danish market (Jobindex, Jobnet, Akademikernes Jobbank, etc.), but the pattern is designed to be swapped for your local job boards. ``` /setup /scrape /apply | | | v v v Fill in Search job Evaluate fit your profile portals Score & recommend | | | v v v Profile Present matches Draft CV + Cover Letter files ready with fit ratings (LaTeX, tailored) | | v v Pick a match Reviewer agent critiques -> /apply -> Revise -> Final output ``` The framework encodes career guidance best practices, including structured evaluation criteria, forward-looking cover letter framing, and optional salary benchmarking. ## Prerequisites - [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) (CLI). Claude Code has no free tier: you need a Claude Pro/Max/Team subscription or Anthropic API credits (pay-per-token, usually cheaper for occasional use). Using a different agent tool (Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI)? Start at [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) - the portal search skills work there out of the box, and [community forks](https://github.com/MadsLorentzen/ai-job-search/discussions/78) adapt the full workflow. - Python 3.10+ - [Bun](https://bun.sh) (for job search CLI tools) - LaTeX distribution with `lualatex` and `xelatex`: [TeX Live](https://tug.org/texlive/), [MacTeX](https://tug.org/mactex/), [TinyTeX](https://yihui.org/tinytex/), or [MiKTeX](https://miktex.org/). The CV compiles with `lualatex` (pdflatex often fails on modern MiKTeX installs with `fontawesome5` font-expansion errors); the cover letter compiles with `xelatex` because `cover.cls` requires `fontspec`. If using a minimal TeX install such as TinyTeX or BasicTeX, install the extra packages listed in [SETUP.md](SETUP.md#minimal-tex-install-tinytexbasictex). - Optional: `pip install pypdf` for `/apply`'s ATS parseability check (BSD; no Poppler required). Poppler `pdftotext` remains a fallback (macOS: `brew install poppler`, Debian/Ubuntu: `apt install poppler-utils`, Windows: `choco install poppler`). If both are missing, the check degrades to a visual keyword review. ## Quick start > 🎥 **Prefer to see it in action first?** [The Next New Thing did a hands-on walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HoVxjMNFYv4) of how the workflow is actually used, from setup to a finished application (recorded August 2026 - commands may have evolved since). ### 1. Fork and clone ```bash gh repo fork MadsLorentzen/ai-job-search --clone cd ai-job-search ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > **A fork of this repo is always public** — GitHub does not allow private forks of > public repositories — and `/setup` (step 3 below) writes your personal data (name, > contact details, employment history, salary expectations) into **tracked** files. > If this copy is for your own job search rather than for contributing changes back, > use a **private repository** with this repo as `upstream` instead — the two-minute > recipe is in [SETUP.md section 8](SETUP.md#8-pulling-upstream-updates-into-your-fork), > and every update workflow works identically. Fork only to contribute. ### 2. Install job search tools ```bash python3 tools/install_portal_clis.py # Windows: python tools\install_portal_clis.py ``` It runs `bun install` in every portal CLI under `.agents/skills/*/cli/` - discovered, not listed, so a portal you add with `/add-portal` or copy from another fork is included on a fresh clone. A CLI whose `package.json` declares an install-time lifecycle script is skipped and reported rather than run. `--dry-run` shows what it would install. For `linkedin-search` and `freehire-search` the install is optional: both have zero runtime dependencies and run with plain `bun`; `bun install` only pulls TypeScript dev types. ### 3. Set up your profile ```bash claude # Then inside Claude Code: /setup ``` `/setup` offers three paths: read your `documents/` folder if you have one populated (CV PDF, LinkedIn export, diplomas, reference letters, past applications), import a single CV pasted in chat, or walk through an interview. It auto-detects what you have and asks. Documents-folder mode is idempotent and safe to re-run as you add more material; see `documents/README.md` for the layout. ### 4. Search for jobs ```bash /scrape ``` This searches multiple job portals for positions matching your profile, deduplicates results, and presents them sorted by fit. Pick a match to run `/apply` on it directly — or, when a scrape returns more jobs than you want to eyeball, run `/rank` to batch-score them all against the fit framework and get a ranked shortlist first. ### 5. Apply to a job ```bash /apply https://jobindex.dk/job/1234567 ``` If the URL can't be fetched (some job portals block automated access), you can paste the job description directly instead: ```bash /apply ``` This runs the full workflow: evaluate fit, draft CV + cover letter, review with a second agent, revise, and present the final output. Postings are treated as untrusted input (the workflow follows no instructions embedded in them and fetches no links from their body), but agentic defenses are instruction-level, not a sandbox - on an unfamiliar job board, skim what was fetched and written before you hit send.
